chapters.title: Chapter 4: Lagrange Multipliers: Optimization Under Equality Constraints

lessons.title: Case Study: Deriving the Full Efficient Frontier With Two Constraints (Budget and Target Return)

children.text: The interviewer's last question for this round of the process: not just the minimum variance point, the whole efficient frontier from Chapter 1, every target return at once. Two constraints are now active together, a target return and the budget rule, which means two Lagrange multipliers instead of one. The result is more than just a bigger calculation. It reveals a genuinely elegant structure hiding inside the whole family of efficient portfolios.

body.text: With two constraints, the Lagrangian needs two multipliers, one per constraint. Solving it reveals that every efficient portfolio, at every target return, is built from combining just two fixed vectors in different proportions. Only the mix changes as the target return changes, never the two building blocks themselves.

body.caption: One multiplier for the return target, one for the budget rule. Same construction as Lesson 1, just one more constraint term.

children.text: The Stationarity Condition Reveals a Two-Fund Structure

body.caption: Every solution is a weighted combination of exactly two fixed vectors, Σ⁻¹μ and Σ⁻¹1.

body.text: This is the two-fund separation result, one of the most quoted facts in portfolio theory. Sigma inverse mu and Sigma inverse 1 never change, no matter what target return you ask for. Only a and b change. In practice, this means a fund does not need to re-run a full optimization for every client's risk target. Compute Sigma inverse mu and Sigma inverse 1 exactly once, then blend them in different proportions to serve any target return on the entire frontier.

children.text: Plug w = aΣ⁻¹μ + bΣ⁻¹1 back into both constraints. Three scalar quantities fall out naturally, each a dot product of the two building-block vectors.

body.latex: A = \mathbf{1}^T\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}, \quad B = \boldsymbol{\mu}^T\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol{\mu}, \quad C = \mathbf{1}^T\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1} \quad \Rightarrow \quad aB + bA = R^*, \;\; aA + bC = 1
body.caption: A two-equation, two-unknown system in a and b, regardless of how many assets are in the portfolio.

body.latex: D = BC - A^2 \qquad a = \frac{R^*C - A}{D}, \qquad b = \frac{B - R^*A}{D}
body.caption: Solved directly by Cramer's rule.

children.text: Numeric Case Study: Reliance, TCS, HDFC Bank at a 15% Target Return
Reuse Σ⁻¹1 ≈ (6.724, 13.273, 9.803), already solved in the previous lesson. The only new ingredient needed is Σ⁻¹μ, using μ = (0.14, 0.16, 0.15), the same expected returns from Chapter 1.

body.title: Show me the elimination for Σ⁻¹μ

content.caption: Solving Σy = μ, using the exact same elimination multipliers as the previous lesson, since the left-hand side matrix is identical.
After eliminating y2. Back-substitution gives the remaining two entries.

body.latex: A \approx 4.535, \quad B \approx 0.6942, \quad C \approx 29.800, \quad D = BC - A^2 \approx 0.1179
body.caption: The three scalar dot products and the resulting determinant D.
Solving the 2x2 system for the target return R* = 0.15.
Combine the two building-block vectors in the proportions a and b.

children.text: Confirming This Traces the Efficient Frontier

Change the target return, and only a and b need recalculating, a tiny 2x2 solve. Sigma inverse mu and Sigma inverse 1 never need to be touched again. Try R* = 0.16, TCS's own individual expected return.

body.caption: The exact same formula, only R* changed.
At 16% target return, the frontier portfolio shorts Reliance by about 16.8% to fund an overweight position in TCS.

body.text: Pushing the target return up toward the best individual stock's own return, here TCS at 16%, forces the unconstrained frontier to short something else to stay fully invested while chasing that return. This is the same equality-constraints-only limitation from the previous lesson, now showing up naturally as you walk along the frontier rather than in a specially constructed example. A fund with a real no-short-selling mandate cannot actually reach every point this frontier describes. Chapter 5's KKT conditions are what correctly reshape the frontier once that rule is enforced.

body.title: Apply the two-fund formula
body.question: Using this lesson's constants, A ≈ 4.535, B ≈ 0.6942, C ≈ 29.800, D ≈ 0.1179, what is a for a target return of R* = 0.16?
body.explanation: a = (R*C - A) / D = ((0.16)(29.800) - 4.535) / 0.1179 = (4.768 - 4.535) / 0.1179 = 0.233 / 0.1179 ≈ 1.974, matching the value this lesson used when it pushed the target return to 16% and found the frontier portfolio shorting Reliance.

body.title: Use two-fund separation operationally
body.scenario: A robo-advisory platform wants to offer clients ten different risk-target portfolios, from conservative to aggressive, all built from the same universe of 40 stocks.
body.prompt: Using this lesson's two-fund separation result, how could the platform generate all ten portfolios efficiently, without running ten separate full optimizations?
body.modelAnswer: The platform can compute Σ⁻¹μ and Σ⁻¹1 exactly once for the 40-stock universe, the expensive matrix-inversion step. Each of the ten target returns then only requires solving the small 2x2 system for a and b, using the same A, B, C, D scalars derived once from those two vectors, and combining w = aΣ⁻¹μ + bΣ⁻¹1. This turns ten expensive optimizations into one matrix inversion plus ten cheap 2x2 solves, exactly the computational advantage the two-fund separation result provides.

body.label: Two-fund separation
body.context: Every efficient portfolio, at every target return, is a combination of just these two fixed vectors. Only a and b, solved from a small 2x2 system, change with the target return.

body.title: The Efficient Frontier via Two Multipliers: Core Terms

cards.definition: L = f(w) - λ1(g1(w) - c1) - λ2(g2(w) - c2), one multiplier per constraint, extending directly from the single-constraint case.
The result that every point on the efficient frontier is a linear combination of exactly two fixed vectors, Σ⁻¹μ and Σ⁻¹1, with only the mix changing across target returns.
Scalar dot products of the two building-block vectors (A = 1ᵀΣ⁻¹μ, B = μᵀΣ⁻¹μ, C = 1ᵀΣ⁻¹1, D = BC - A²) used to solve the small 2x2 system for a and b at any target return.

points: Two active constraints need two Lagrange multipliers, but the stationarity condition reveals every efficient portfolio is aΣ⁻¹μ + bΣ⁻¹1, a combination of just two fixed vectors.
a and b solve from a small 2x2 linear system built from three scalars, A, B, and C, computed once from the covariance matrix and expected returns.
Changing the target return only requires re-solving that small 2x2 system, never re-inverting the covariance matrix, a major computational advantage for generating many portfolios along the frontier.
For Reliance, TCS, and HDFC Bank at a 15% target return, the frontier portfolio is roughly 33.57% Reliance, 33.93% TCS, and 32.50% HDFC Bank.

Pushing the target return higher, toward or past the best individual stock's own return, forces the unconstrained frontier to short something, the same limitation from the previous lesson, now visible directly on the frontier.

Chapter 4 is complete: the Lagrangian, why it works geometrically, what the multiplier means, and how it scales to any number of assets and multiple constraints. Chapter 5 extends this machinery to handle inequality constraints like no-short-selling directly, via KKT conditions.
